nameStory: The Eastern Tiger Swallowtail gets its name from the bold black stripes that streak across its bright yellow wings, just like a tiger's markings! The 'swallowtail' part comes from the distinctive tail-like projections on its hindwings that resemble the forked tail of a swallow bird.
description: The Eastern Tiger Swallowtail is one of New England's most recognizable butterflies, with its impressive wingspan reaching up to 5.5 inches across. Males are bright yellow with bold black tiger stripes, while females come in two forms - either yellow like the males or dramatically dark black. These large, graceful butterflies are a common sight from spring through fall, gliding through gardens, parks, and woodland edges. Their size and distinctive wing shape make them easy to spot even from a distance.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Look for four distinct black stripes running vertically across each bright yellow forewing - these bold 'tiger stripes' are unmistakable and give the butterfly its name

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: One of our largest butterflies with a wingspan that can span your entire hand, featuring the characteristic 'tails' extending from the hindwings like tiny streamers

idTips.label: Female Color Forms
idTips.description: Females may be either yellow with tiger stripes (like males) plus a band of blue spots along the hindwing edge, or almost entirely black with subtle blue markings

idTips.label: Flight Style
idTips.description: Flies with slow, graceful wing beats and tends to glide more than flutter - watch for their leisurely, sailing flight pattern high above flowers

idTips.label: Caterpillar Appearance
idTips.description: Large green caterpillars (up to 2 inches long) with two prominent false eyespots on the front end that look like a snake's face when threatened

habitat: Eastern Tiger Swallowtails thrive in a variety of New England habitats including suburban gardens, parks, woodland edges, and areas near streams or ponds. They're especially drawn to places where their host plants grow - wild cherry, tulip trees, and magnolias - combined with nectar sources like lilacs, butterfly bush, and wildflowers. You'll often spot them in sunny openings within or adjacent to deciduous forests.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with the first generation appearing in May. Look for fresh, bright yellow butterflies visiting early blooming flowers like lilacs and wild cherry blossoms.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs during summer months when you'll see both the continuing first generation and fresh second-generation butterflies. This is the best time to observe mating behavior and egg-laying on host plants.
seasonality.fall: A third generation may emerge in late summer through early fall, though these butterflies are typically smaller. Caterpillars are actively feeding and growing larger before forming chrysalises for winter.
seasonality.winter: Butterflies overwinter as chrysalises attached to tree branches or other surfaces, appearing as brown, leaf-like cases that blend into their surroundings until spring emergence.

funFact: When threatened, Tiger Swallowtail caterpillars can instantly transform into convincing snake mimics by inflating their front segment to display huge fake eyespots, complete with realistic pupils, while rearing up and swaying menacingly - a performance so believable it can fool birds and even humans!
confusionNotes: The dark female form is often mistaken for a Spicebush Swallowtail, but Tiger Swallowtail females are noticeably larger and lack the prominent orange spots that Spicebush Swallowtails display. Remember: 'Tiger size trumps Spicebush spots' - if it's really big and mostly black, it's likely a female Tiger Swallowtail.
contextualKnowledge: This beloved butterfly serves as the official state butterfly for five southeastern states and state insect for Virginia, making it one of the most honored insects in America. The dramatic difference between yellow and black female forms exists because the dark females mimic the toxic Pipevine Swallowtail to avoid predation.
compareHints: Among New England's swallowtails, Eastern Tiger Swallowtails are the largest and most boldly striped when yellow. Black Swallowtails are smaller with blue and orange spots rather than stripes, while Spicebush Swallowtails have prominent orange markings and are noticeably smaller. Canadian Tiger Swallowtails are nearly identical but generally found further north and lack the dark female form.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's swallowtails, Black Swallowtails are the most 'polka-dotted' with their precise yellow spots, while Eastern Tiger Swallowtails are predominantly yellow with black stripes, and Spicebush Swallowtails have greenish-blue highlights with blurry pale markings.
Among New England's swallowtails, spicebush swallowtails are the darkest and most consistently black, lacking the yellow stripes of tiger swallowtails or the yellow spot-bands of black swallowtails.

Unlike the Black Swallowtail which is much smaller and primarily black with blue markings, or the Spicebush Swallowtail which has more blue-green iridescence, the Canadian Tiger Swallowtail maintains its yellow and black tiger pattern in both sexes.
Compared to the Eastern Tiger Swallowtail, the midsummer species has a distinct later flight period and is often slightly smaller with more vivid coloration.
